The post Review: High West Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
High West makes a bevy of luxe whiskeys, such as Bourye, The Prisoner’s Share, and A Midwinter Night’s Dram, but it’s also been expanding its presence on lower shelves, the most basic of the bunch being this otherwise unadorned bourbon, the simplest and least expensive bottle in its arsenal.

Some of the contents are disclosed, some arent. What we do know is that it’s a blend of mashbills from various locations, including a 75% corn, 21% rye, 4% malted barley offering from MGP; an 84% corn, 8% rye, 8% malted barley bourbon from parts unknown, and “other whiskey components undisclosed due to contractual reasons.”

None of this carries an age statement.

We got a bottle. Let’s check it out.

High West Bourbon Review

The immediate rush of peanut and popcorn should come as no big surprise; this is clearly young stuff that feels like walking into a Cracker Jack factory. Simplistic and a little leathery, the whiskey never finds much more to grab on to beyond this basic introduction.

The palate isn’t much more expressive, heavy on peanut and actually a little bitter, with slightly musty overtones reminscent of old books and roast beef. Time in glass fortunately helps some of the more rustic elements to blow off, ultimately revealing a sharp but moderated citrus note perking up on the finish. Largely anonymous, but at least it’s affordable.

90 proof. Reviewed: Batch#24C13.

B- / $38 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Garrison Brothers Ranch Reserve Bourbon – Oloroso and PX
summary:

As is traditional for many Garrison Brothers releases, both of these whiskeys spend four years in new American white oak barrels before…

The post Review: Garrison Brothers Ranch Reserve Bourbon – Oloroso and PX appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Ready for a twist from Texas icons Garrison Bros.? The Texas icons have launched a pair of new releases called Ranch Reserve — bourbons finished in oloroso sherry and PX sherry casks, respectively.

As is traditional for many Garrison Brothers releases, both of these whiskeys spend four years in new American white oak barrels before finishing in a sherry cask (either oloroso or PX, natch) — both of which offer a lengthy four years of finishing time, making these 8 year old expressions.

Garrison works regularly with Port casks, but not so much with sherry. How will delicate, wine-forward sherry contrast with the heavy Texasness of Garrison Brothers bourbon? Let’s find out.

Also of note: “PX and Oloroso Sherry Cask Finished, as part of the Ranch Reserve Series, showcase a brand-new bottle design. The front of the bottle bears a designed leather band and walnut colored wax dipping. The “Ranch Reserve” label will be prominently featured. Each expression produced 6,000 bottles. Both will be first available at the distillery and then online and in select markets to follow.” (Single barrel versions have also been announced.)

Garrison Brothers Ranch Reserve Bourbon Oloroso Review

The nose plays things a bit tight: This still has the aggressive woodiness and frontier funk of classic Garrison Bros. expressions, but it’s lightened up just so, with an exotic twist on the nose that evokes incense and saffron. It’s altogether unique for Garrison Brothers. I honestly can’t think of another whiskey from the operation that has quite this level of heady, aromatic heft.

The palate follows the theme — first a punch of hard, fresh oak, followed by a tempering note of floral incense. It’s quite a bizarre twist for a Garrison Bros. product, a chewy sweetness building as the body develops, ultimately evoking notes of toasted coconut, milk chocolate, and a touch of menthol. Increasingly minty on the finish, the whiskey winds its way away from sherry and toward duskier, huskier territory. As things develop, coffee and cherry notes become more prominent and sustained, with a curious hint of pistachio and ample, lingering chocolate on the finish. Definitely a twist on the GB formula. 110 proof. B+ / $150

Garrison Brothers Ranch Reserve Bourbon PX Review

For all the wine and fruit in the Oloroso expression, the PX version blows that out of the water. Stick your nose in the glass and it perks up right away: intensely nutty, leathery, raisiny, it’s a heady experience that pours on baking spice notes, especially cloves and ginger, all filtered through a thick skein of oak charred black.

The palate tells a similar story. Quite sweet and wholly wine-soaked, lush with raisins but more prominently dates and dried figs. Candied and laced with caramel and chocolate, this is one of the most decadent Garrison Brothers whiskeys I’ve ever encountered. Thick and unctuous, the whiskey drapes over the tongue like oil, turning toward maple syrup and more chocolate sauce as it develops. “Luxurious” is a word used by Garrison Bros. to describe this experience, and it couldn’t be more perfect.

The decadence and sweetness don’t last forever. Eventually the whiskey has to come back down to earth, where a sharper, wood-driven character awaits. That Texas heat can only be ignored for so long, and the conclusion is hot and tight, tannic oak rearing back like a bronco. Water helps to tame that finish, but it also perforates what comes before, dulling the fruit, taking the whole affair down a notch. Be careful with your water dosage, and you may well find yourself with a transcendent experience. 109 proof. A- / $150

The post Review: Mezcal El Silencio Espadin appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
This was the first line extension of Mezcal El Silencio after its original Ensamble launch, this one made in San Baltazar, Oaxaca exclusively from espadin agave. The black bottle is inspired by Oaxaca’s barro negro pottery and is certainly striking on the shelf.

Let’s give it a whirl.

Mezcal El Silencio Espadin Review

Designed to be softer and less overtly smoky, this expression of El Silencio is true to its claims, more subtle on the nose than many modern mezcal expressions but certainly still part of the mezcal family, featuring notes of browning grass and creosote backed by a mix of dried herbs and hints of dark chocolate.

While the nose is quite savory, the palate finds a little sweetness, that chocolate emerging as touched with brown sugar and honey, some notes of cherry juice working their way into the mix. The spirit evolves in glass to reveal some of the salinity featured in the Ensamble release, particularly on the surprisingly lengthy finish. A spritz of lemon peel brightens up the outro, some sweetened mint syrup lingering on the conclusion.

It’s definitely a step up from the Ensamble and — good news — a significant price cut makes it much more appealing in its competitive space.

86 proof. NOM-AMMA78. Reviewed: Lot #001-25AM.

B+ / $38

title: Review: Suavecito Tequila Extra Anejo
summary:
Our first look at Suavecito was last year when Chris explored an Anejo Single Barrel that, on paper, is a bit of an outlier from the brand’s core lineup. The name Suavecito translates to “smooth” and shows up on every label in the portfolio outside of the single barrel expressions which, by Chris’s estimation, are…

The post Review: Suavecito Tequila Extra Anejo appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Our first look at Suavecito was last year when Chris explored an Anejo Single Barrel that, on paper, is a bit of an outlier from the brand’s core lineup. The name Suavecito translates to “smooth” and shows up on every label in the portfolio outside of the single barrel expressions which, by Chris’s estimation, are perhaps a bit too bold and dry to merit the descriptor.

Today, we’re looking at the tippy top of the “smoother” Suavecito offerings, an extra anejo made from 100% blue agave and aged in retired American oak bourbon barrels for an impressive five years – two years longer than required for the category. Like the rest of the non-single barrel Suavecito lineup, this isn’t technically a tequila by American standards due to its proof (70 proof is allowed in Mexico but 80 proof is the minimum in the U.S.). It also contains up to 2% unfermented agave nectar collected after roasting. Thoughts follow.

Suavecito Tequila Extra Anejo Review

The aroma is gentle and honeyed with notes of agave syrup, stewed peppers, and split vanilla bean. It’s sweet but not overly so, which is a bit surprising given the extended barrel aging and the addition of the agave nectar. Extra anejos can be butterscotch bombs, but this is almost closer to a standard anejo in profile with just a bit more bourbon barrel sweetness in the mix. As it opens, the savory notes bloom a bit more, adding some bell pepper and roasted agave to the bouquet.

The palate is where Suavecito’s mission for “smooth” really shows; for good and maybe not so good if you’re a tequila purist. This is a creamy, saccharine tequila that delivers zero hint of alcohol and little in the way of spiritous warmth. The sweetness is kept in check just enough to avoid being cloying but only just barely. Notes of dark honey, vanilla taffy, and agave syrup reinforce a dessert-like profile from sip to swallow. The midpalate manages to deliver a hint of coffee bean and a cooked agave note that is vaguely herbal before dissolving into a syrupy, gently peppery finish that is just short enough to keep the sweetness from feeling heavy. Suavecito makes no excuses for putting texture and temperature above flavor in their mission for the “smoothest” tequila. Purists probably aren’t their target audience, but there is probably enough flavor here for the occasional tequila drinker to appreciate. Its biggest fans will be newcomers to the category. And those with a serious sweet tooth.

70 proof.

B / $130

The post Review: Ferrand Pineau des Charentes Blanc appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Maison Ferrand may be known for making Cognac (and, of course, gin and rum as well), but its latest release isn’t a spirit at all. Ferrand’s new Pineau des Charentes is a fortified wine — and one of the most undersung delicacies of the Cognac region.

If you aren’t familiar, Pineau des Charentes is made in a method similar to Port, where freshly pressed grape must is fortified with Cognac before fermentation is complete, leaving the finished product naturally sweet and a little boozier than table wine. Ferrand’s is aged for a minimum of 18 months in oak barrels before bottling at 17% abv.

We received a bottle and put it through its paces.

Ferrand Pineau des Charentes Blanc Review

Pineau is always a treat to sample, and Ferrand’s is no exception. A bright nose exudes notes of mixed florals, honeyed pear, some citrus, and finally almonds, providing a truly beautiful collection of aromas to stick your nose into. As you sip, the initially floral-heavy wine leans more into the fruit, first lemon, then Meyer lemon, then tangerine. Soon, the affair turns peachy as the sweetness builds, finishing with a touch of apricot and a light hint of mint.

All told, it’s as delightful a bottle of Pineau as I can recall tasting in recent years. At this price, snap it up and sip it straight or mix it with tonic for an autumnal treat.

17% abv.

A- / $34

Today we’re looking at three of them, including a fruity bottled old fashioned and a pair of finished whiskeys. Penelope Architects of Golf Hole 01 Review The whiskey world loves no sport more than golf, so leave…

The post Review: Penelope Masters of Golf Hole 01, Riviera, and Blackberry Old Fashioned appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Penelope has been extremely busy of late, putting out new whiskeys and RTD cocktails at a rapid clip. Today we’re looking at three of them, including a fruity bottled old fashioned and a pair of finished whiskeys.

Penelope Architects of Golf Hole 01 Review

The whiskey world loves no sport more than golf, so leave it to Penelope to start a new series of whiskeys that will probably end up spanning 18 editions, or “Holes,” in the parlance of the brand. Three holes have been dropped from the start, each a 6 year old straight bourbon distinguished by a unique spin on its finishing technique. All three expressions are made from a 60% corn, 36% rye, 4% barley mashbill and were finished with additional American oak staves (a la Maker’s 46), the only difference among them being the length of the finishing time, which is measured in weeks. However, Penelope doesn’t disclose that finishing time for any of the offerings. In any case, we received only Hole 01 for review.

It’s a surprisingly lively and, at times, decadent bourbon, the stave finishing clearly having an outsized impact. The nose is bold and quite oak-forward, peppery and a touch smoky, but also big with cloves and grains with a heavy toast. Time in glass perks up a surprising fruit overtone — slightly pruny, with a dark chocolate glaze — which adds some lovely nuance to what could otherwise be a barrel-heavy experience.

The palate definitely drinks older than 6 years of age, smoldering chocolate and vanilla pushy against, again, a hefty fruitiness — blueberry, blackberry, touched with baking spice. This is one of those whiskeys that shifts fairly heavily as the finish arrives, becoming quite savory again, laden with wood and notes of furniture polish, then swinging back, at least a bit, toward anise and darker spice notes, with a reprise of clove and some anise.

I didn’t think this golf-themed whiskey was going to amount to much, but damn if it doesn’t make me want to pick up a 3-iron. 94 proof. A- / $80

Penelope Riviera Review

Riviera is the latest addition to Penelope Bourbon’s Cooper Series. It’s made by blending an 8-year-old American light whiskey with straight bourbon (no age stated), and is finished in rosé wine casks from Spain. If you remember Penelope Rose Cask Finish, this is something of a sequel (though Rose Cask Finish was a bourbon).

Riviera isn’t quite as delightful, a heavily charred nose giving the aromatics a thick smear of toasty wood, mildly smoky at times and heavy with gravelly asphalt notes and, curiously, a healthy touch of menthol. I’ll be quick to note that Rose Cask had a lot of the same aromas, but that things livened up quickly on its palate, showcasing effusive cherry and chocolate notes. There’s a lot of that here, but it takes longer to show its face, the woodiness maintaining long-term dominance. Eventually, the finish brightens up and pours on that fruit, offering more of a maraschino cherry overtone than anything else. It’s a close #2 to the original, but my heart still lies with the forebear. 94 proof. B+ / $80

Penelope Blackberry Old Fashioned Review

A fruity foil to Penelope’s Black Walnut Old Fashioned, this one really does wear those berries on its sleeve. The punch of blackberry isn’t entirely distinct, however. This could be a mix of blackberry with raspberry, strawberry, currant, and/or blueberry, but it’s really the dessert-like thought that counts, I suppose. Ample waves of chocolate and vanilla serve to temper the fruit before its sweetness gets out of control — though there’s a summery punch of maraschino cherry on the finish that feels perfectly on point with what’s come before. Simple, summertime sipping here. 38 proof. A- / $25

title: Review: Independence Brewing Native Texan and Oklahoma Suks
summary:
Independence Brewing was founded by two University of Texas alumni, so it makes sense that the founders would support the home team on this, the eve of 122nd edition of the Red River Rivalry against the University of Oklahoma, held annually at the Cotton Bowl in Dallas. But Independence bleeds burnt orange so much that…

The post Review: Independence Brewing Native Texan and Oklahoma Suks appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Independence Brewing was founded by two University of Texas alumni, so it makes sense that the founders would support the home team on this, the eve of 122nd edition of the Red River Rivalry against the University of Oklahoma, held annually at the Cotton Bowl in Dallas. But Independence bleeds burnt orange so much that they even put out to memorialize that rivalry, particularly the hatred for all things Oklahoma — a distaste that runs so thick that “OU Sucks!” is unofficially part of the Texas fight song.

Today we pour fresh pints of Independence’s most visible year-round offering, Native Texan, as well as the OU brew.

Independence Brewing Native Texan Review

Closer to a German style pilsner, with Hallertau Mittelfrüh hops pumped up to 36 IBUs. Brisk and foamy, this is a boldly malty beer that could well be Bavarian if you didn’t see the label, with a big pretzelly character that really fills the mouth. Light lemon and some cardamom notes sneak in as the beer warms up, the citrus becoming increasingly prominent as the finish arrives. Chewy but well-rounded, it’s touched with enough nuance to work whether it’s Oktoberfest or not. 5.2% abv. A- / $10 per six-pack

Independence Brewing Oklahoma Suks Review

A standard pilsner with a lighter sprinkling of Hallertau Mittelfrüh hops (just 10 IBUs). Considerably more straightforward, here the malt and cereal do all the heavy lifting, which leaves you with a rather sweet finish to deal with that ends up a little one note. Tasted side by side, the hops in Native Texan pull more of their weight than it originally seems, and Oklahoma Suks leaves the game with an overtly doughy, almost gummy quality on the tongue. Perhaps, of course, that’s the intent. Best enjoyed with a side of OU vs. Georgia highlights. 5% abv. B / $10 per six-pack

title: Review: Tequilas of Dos Hombres (Updated 2026)
summary:
In 2022, we covered the launch of Dos Hombres, a then exclusively mezcal brand backed by actors Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. At the time, we tipped our hat to the Breaking Bad stars for the super cool way they chose to focus on mezcal instead of the more ubiquitous and celebrity-saturated tequila category. But…

The post Review: Tequilas of Dos Hombres (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
In 2022, we covered the launch of Dos Hombres, a then exclusively mezcal brand backed by actors Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. At the time, we tipped our hat to the Breaking Bad stars for the super cool way they chose to focus on mezcal instead of the more ubiquitous and celebrity-saturated tequila category. But it was only a matter of time. This spring Dos Hombres jumped into the very crowded tequila game. To their credit, the brand is still going about things coolly with the same craft and impressive transparency that they apply to their mezcals.

We received a sample of their inaugural blanco tequila, which is produced in the village of Amatitan at Tequilera TAP Distillery from 100% blue weber agave by veteran Maestro Julio Cova who came out of retirement to guide the Dos Hombres project. The agave is crushed using a roller mill, cooked in a combination of autoclave (75%) and brick ovens (25%), fermented for an unusually long 72-96 hours, and then double distilled in stainless steel and copper. It rests for 30 days before bottling. Thoughts follow.

Update: Cranston and Paul have unsurprisingly taken the logical next step in tequila succession and added a reposado to the lineup. We’re adding that review here, and will add coverage of the eventual anejo release when it arrives.

Dos Hombres Tequila Blanco Review

Tequila may have been a comparatively boring move for the Breaking Bad boys, but damn if they didn’t nail this blanco. The nose shows some of the most depth I’ve encountered in an unaged tequila with creamy notes of sweet, roasted agave and cinnamon frosting. Undertones of fresh lime zest and grilled lemon add energy and brightness, and with time to open, accents of pink peppercorn further enhance an already warm and enticing aroma.

The palate is crisp and light with notes of mint and white pepper. The agave is unusually fresh in contrast to the typical roasted note you often find in tequila. In place of the traditional agave syrup or roasted pulp notes, this is noticeably brighter and more tropical. The midpalate is crisp and floral with orange oil and rosewater that transitions to freshly grated cinnamon and clove on a long, gently peppery finish. It works great in a classic tequila cocktail like a margarita with that crisp profile working wonders for balance. But it’s almost a shame to mix with it. 80 proof. A / $48 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Dos Hombres Tequila Reposado Review

Like the blanco, this tequila was produced in Amatitan, Jalisco from 100% blue weber agave using 72-96 hour fermentations and double distillation in copper and stainless steel. This expression was then aged a short three months in American oak – reportedly ex-bourbon barrels sourced from the Four Roses Distillery – and cut with deep earth volcanic water (sounds way cooler than “natural spring”). The final product was then allowed to rest a full 30 days in stainless steel to mellow and balance. Let’s check it out.

The nose is remarkable. I didn’t think they could improve on the blanco’s bouquet, but the barrel aging really has accentuated things. Top notes of gently cooked agave are silky and expressive, presenting with a rich, caramelized sweetness underpinned by soft baking spice and brown sugar. The citrus undertones show a surprising amount of freshness for a barrel aged spirit, coming through as just a little more candied than the blanco but still energetic and bright. The peppercorn notes from the unaged expression have softened to white pepper with a hint of smoke and minerality.

The palate is less transformed by the barrel, retaining the purity of this unusually fresh and gently spiced tequila with early notes of split piña, bruised mint, clove syrup, and candied pineapple. A light dusting of cinnamon sugar and notes of ginger snap cookies on the midpalate are the clearest evidence of the barrel aging, and even that gives way on the finish to a sweet, floral fadeout of orange marmalade and rosehip. Despite a memorable nose, I prefer the blanco just a bit more. Still, it’s an impressive next step in the Dos Hombres portfolio, and I look very much forward to sampling the anejo when it arrives. 80 proof. A- / $50

title: The Top 10 Wines for Winter 2027
summary:
For the first time in recent memory, the high temperature for the day was under 90 degrees here. That counts as fall in Austin, Texas, and is enough for us to break out our second top 10 wines list for the year. These 10 selections were picked with cooler weather in mind (and the meals…

The post The Top 10 Wines for Winter 2027 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
For the first time in recent memory, the high temperature for the day was under 90 degrees here. That counts as fall in Austin, Texas, and is enough for us to break out our second top 10 wines list for the year. These 10 selections were picked with cooler weather in mind (and the meals that come with it) – though no one will bat an eye if you pop the cork on one of these before the temperature dips too far (or after it comes back up).

Want to buy them? Remember: Check Total Wine and Wine.com for the best deals on all of these picks! You can also search multiple stores at wine-searcher to find the best prices on all these products and more.

1. 2022 Terrazas de los Andes Extremo Malbec

Argentine malbec exists in two worlds: Affordable but wholly enjoyable entry-level wines on one hand, meticulously produced artisanal products on the other. As the name (and price) suggest, Terrazas de los Andes Extremo Malbec is in the latter camp, a serious wine produced at an altitude over a mile above sea level. The results are something else, a restrained wine that keeps wild herbs on the down low, fruit and oak well-integrated with silky tannin and bright acidity. Gentle spice notes linger on a finish so delightful you’ll forget what you paid for the experience. $200

2. 2023 Sassotondo Monte Calvo Ciliegiolo

Maremma flies a bit under the radar, but you’ll find some of Italy’s most nuanced wines produced in this Tuscan region. This one is made from ciliegiolo grapes (purportedly a progenitor of sangiovese, though this is disputed) which grow in rich volcanic soil. What Sassotondo has done with it is delightful, producing a light-bodied expression of fruity cherries, touched with almonds, flowers, and some peppery spice. While Chianti can be excessively tart, this wine offers a more balanced, almost creamy quality that really holds your attention. $45

3. 2020 Montefili Vigna Nel Bosco Chianti Classico Gran Selezione DOCG

Bosco is Italian for “woods,” and this Chianti Clasico bottling doesn’t just evoke the forest with its name, it also does in the glass. Lightly earthy and dusky, with a mix of green herbs and toasted spices, this smoldering wine moves into slightly sweeter, chocolate-driven character as the finish builds. In the end, the drinker is left with notes of cherry and plum to chew on. $61

4. 2021 Roederer Estate Clark Road Vineyard Anderson Valley

Vintage sparkling wines usually mean shelling out a small fortune for the luxury, but Roederer’s 2021 Clark Road Vineyard offering – 3/4 pinot noir and 1/4 chardonnay – is a delicious exception. One of my favorite wines from the operation, this fruity delight pairs dried apples and toasted almonds with ample salinity and late-game melon, all coming together to show off the delightful, citrus peel-driven finish. Great value. $55

5. 2023 X Novo Pinot Noir X Omni Vineyard

We had our first experience with X Novo this year and are hoping it won’t be the last. This brightly fruit-forward pinot keeps the focus on the purity of the berries, with smoldering terroir becoming increasingly visible as the wine develops in glass. The gentle tannins complement the wine beautifully, and even the touch of balsamic on the finish only serves to amplify the wine’s charms further. Like Cru Burgundy, made in California. $100

6. 2023 Oleandri La Scala Red Wine Napa Valley

This Left Bank Bordeaux-style blend throws a twist into the mix in the form of 4.5% petite sirah, which gives an already aggressive wine even more gravity and density. Nearly black in its opacity, the wine takes its core of currant and cocoa powder and pours on the earthiness, though the wine never approaches anything that tastes green or off. Air improves things further – consider decanting – allowing bright cherry elements to emerge. $80

7. 2023 The Prisoner Grail Stags Leap District

You surely know The Prisoner as a widely available (and much loved) red blend – but lately the brand has become the spearhead for a wide range of spinoffs, the latest being The Prisoner Grail, a luxe cabernet blend that approaches a whopping $200. It’s made from fruit from one of the most prized vineyards in Napa, Wappo Hill, and the significantly boozy wine doesn’t pull any punches. Bold currant, blackberry, and blueberry notes inform a very dense, undulating experience that is, quite naturally, balanced by gently tannic tobacco and graphite notes. The wine’s complexity never really ends, even as the finish finally fades out. $200

8. 2023 Prats + Symington Chryseia Douro DOC

Portugal is known for cheap whites and expensive Ports, but Chryseia stands as one of the country’s most noteworthy red table wines. A blend of Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca, the wine can stand up against any of the icons of the Old World, its elegant body driven by plum and cherry en route to a more brambly, slightly ashy finish. The structure is just about perfect, while the wine’s intensity is unyielding. $125

9. 2023 The Hilt Estate Chardonnay Santa Rita Hills

For my money, Chardonnay works better when there’s a bit of chill in the air than in the dead of summer, and while this beautiful wine leads with iconic lemon, apple, and pear notes, the fruit settles down into an autumnal groove, ultimately evoking thoughts of apple pie and coconut cream. Never overly woody nor saccharine in the slightest, it offers a clean and versatile experience that works both as a happy hour crowd-pleaser and as a mealtime companion. $50 [BUY IT NOW FROM WINE.COM]

10. 2022 Papapietro Perry Pinot Noir Russian River Valley Peters Vineyard

This striking Russian River Pinot dodges the trap that frequently sinks other Pinot Noirs from the region, its low-level notes of tea leaf and cola livened up by effusive cherry and boysenberry flavors, along with a grating of orange peel. The finish’s distinct chocolate and cinnamon notes provide an enchanting denouement to the wine’s lively attack. $69

title: Review: Tequila El Mexicano Anejo
summary:
Tequila El Mexicano, part of Foley Family Wines & Spirits, has finally launched its first anejo. We’ve never covered any of the offerings from the brand, but we’re starting here, with this release that was rested for 14 to 16 months in American and French oak. Agaves are aged a minimum of 6 years and…

The post Review: Tequila El Mexicano Anejo appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Tequila El Mexicano, part of Foley Family Wines & Spirits, has finally launched its first anejo. We’ve never covered any of the offerings from the brand, but we’re starting here, with this release that was rested for 14 to 16 months in American and French oak. Agaves are aged a minimum of 6 years and are grown in the Jalisco Highlands. The Master Tequilero behind the brand is León Bañuelos Sr., son of Tequila Cazadores cofounder Don Félix Bañuelos.

Some more distillation details: “The family uses a careful two-stage ‘low and slow’ cooking method in stainless steel autoclaves for up to 24 hours. Their unique seven-day open-air fermentation – one of the longest in modern tequila production – is enhanced by classical music, stimulating the natural yeast growth. While most distilleries employ copper stills, León Sr. designed stainless steel pot stills to double distill El Mexicano, preserving the agave’s true flavor.”

Tequila El Mexicano Anejo Review

The short of it is that this is an extremely soft tequila, something I’d probably chalk up to the use of French oak in the aging process. Any peppery agave notes on the nose are immediately tempered, showing more cinnamon and nutmeg, well-doused in brown butter. A vague note of chocolate and some coffee elements ring the edges of the experience, giving the experience something of a Sunday pastry vibe.

The palate follows suit, almost to a T. Soft and infused with baking spice, the tequila feels like a caramel glaze intended to be drizzled over a flan or a gingery cake, only less overtly sweet. There’s plenty of sugar in the mix, but it’s tempered with ground coffee, bittersweet cocoa powder, and a light skin of barrel char. An element of brown banana becomes prominent as the finish builds, with a reprise of spice roaring back into the picture as the experience concludes. Curiously, the fade-out is a bit gravelly and earthy, which helps further to temper the up-front sweetness but which doesn’t entirely play to the tequila’s biggest strengths.

80 proof. NOM 1588.

B / $50 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Heaven Hill Bottled-in-Bond Double Mash Bourbon 9 Years Old
summary:
When Heaven Hill re-launched their beloved, namesake Bottled-in-Bond Bourbon back in 2019, they gave it a shiny new label, added another year to the age statement, and tripled the original price. In no time, it became something of a whipping boy for the steady increase in American whiskey prices that, we now know, was just…

The post Review: Heaven Hill Bottled-in-Bond Double Mash Bourbon 9 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
When Heaven Hill re-launched their beloved, namesake Bottled-in-Bond Bourbon back in 2019, they gave it a shiny new label, added another year to the age statement, and tripled the original price. In no time, it became something of a whipping boy for the steady increase in American whiskey prices that, we now know, was just getting started. By comparison to many other bottles on the shelf, Heaven Hill’s Bottled-in-Bond is a relative bargain today.

That shifting landscape may have been a factor in the recent, and somewhat unexpected, addition to Heaven Hill’s Bottled-in-Bond lineup, Double Mash. As the name suggests, this bourbon is a blend of two different mashbills; Heaven Hill’s classic low-rye recipe (78% corn, 10% rye, and 12% malted barley) found in the original Bottled-in-Bond (and pretty much every other rye bourbon in the portfolio) and their wheated mashbill (68% corn, 20% wheat, and 12% malted barley) which features in Larceny and Old Fitzgerald. Both whiskeys were aged for at least nine years before blending, with the wheated portion comprising roughly one third of the final bourbon recipe. Thoughts follow.

Heaven Hill Bottled-in-Bond Double Mash Bourbon 9 Years Old Review

The nose is a bit soft, even with time to open, which is somewhat unexpected given the proof and age. It’s still expressive though, bready and gently sweet with warm notes of apple muffins, cinnamon sugar, and seasoned oak. Time in the glass adds some texture with buttery toffee, Demerara syrup, and undertones of caramel apple. It takes a little patience and effort, but there’s plenty here to admire.

The palate is also impressively approachable, to the point of feeling thin at times, especially on the finish. Still, it delivers enough flavor to hold attention. Early notes of honey butter, corn bread, and orange creamsicle give way on the midpalate to stewed apple and pie spice. It’s silky and builds with brown sugar sweetness into the midpalate before eroding into a medium finish of orange blossom honey, caramel candies, old oak, and warm baking spice. Critics might say it isn’t full-flavored enough for the numbers on the bottle, but I find it just as enjoyable as the classic offering. And there’s something about the mellow profile and subtler flavors in Double Mash that is reminiscent of those legendary, pre-fire years when Heaven Hill Bottled-in-Bond was well-aged, a little funky, and still exceptionally easy drinking.

100 proof.

A- / $50 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: High West Bourbon
summary:
High West makes a bevy of luxe whiskeys, such as Bourye, The Prisoner’s Share, and A Midwinter Night’s Dram, but it’s also been expanding its presence on lower shelves, the most basic of the bunch being this otherwise unadorned bourbon, the simplest and least expensive bottle in its arsenal. Some of the contents are disclosed,…

The post Review: High West Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
High West makes a bevy of luxe whiskeys, such as Bourye, The Prisoner’s Share, and A Midwinter Night’s Dram, but it’s also been expanding its presence on lower shelves, the most basic of the bunch being this otherwise unadorned bourbon, the simplest and least expensive bottle in its arsenal.

Some of the contents are disclosed, some arent. What we do know is that it’s a blend of mashbills from various locations, including a 75% corn, 21% rye, 4% malted barley offering from MGP; an 84% corn, 8% rye, 8% malted barley bourbon from parts unknown, and “other whiskey components undisclosed due to contractual reasons.”

None of this carries an age statement.

We got a bottle. Let’s check it out.

High West Bourbon Review

The immediate rush of peanut and popcorn should come as no big surprise; this is clearly young stuff that feels like walking into a Cracker Jack factory. Simplistic and a little leathery, the whiskey never finds much more to grab on to beyond this basic introduction.

The palate isn’t much more expressive, heavy on peanut and actually a little bitter, with slightly musty overtones reminscent of old books and roast beef. Time in glass fortunately helps some of the more rustic elements to blow off, ultimately revealing a sharp but moderated citrus note perking up on the finish. Largely anonymous, but at least it’s affordable.

90 proof. Reviewed: Batch#24C13.

B- / $38 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Garrison Brothers Ranch Reserve Bourbon – Oloroso and PX
summary:
Ready for a twist from Texas icons Garrison Bros.? The Texas icons have launched a pair of new releases called Ranch Reserve — bourbons finished in oloroso sherry and PX sherry casks, respectively. As is traditional for many Garrison Brothers releases, both of these whiskeys spend four years in new American white oak barrels before…

The post Review: Garrison Brothers Ranch Reserve Bourbon – Oloroso and PX appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Ready for a twist from Texas icons Garrison Bros.? The Texas icons have launched a pair of new releases called Ranch Reserve — bourbons finished in oloroso sherry and PX sherry casks, respectively.

As is traditional for many Garrison Brothers releases, both of these whiskeys spend four years in new American white oak barrels before finishing in a sherry cask (either oloroso or PX, natch) — both of which offer a lengthy four years of finishing time, making these 8 year old expressions.

Garrison works regularly with Port casks, but not so much with sherry. How will delicate, wine-forward sherry contrast with the heavy Texasness of Garrison Brothers bourbon? Let’s find out.

Also of note: “PX and Oloroso Sherry Cask Finished, as part of the Ranch Reserve Series, showcase a brand-new bottle design. The front of the bottle bears a designed leather band and walnut colored wax dipping. The “Ranch Reserve” label will be prominently featured. Each expression produced 6,000 bottles. Both will be first available at the distillery and then online and in select markets to follow.” (Single barrel versions have also been announced.)

Garrison Brothers Ranch Reserve Bourbon Oloroso Review

The nose plays things a bit tight: This still has the aggressive woodiness and frontier funk of classic Garrison Bros. expressions, but it’s lightened up just so, with an exotic twist on the nose that evokes incense and saffron. It’s altogether unique for Garrison Brothers. I honestly can’t think of another whiskey from the operation that has quite this level of heady, aromatic heft.

The palate follows the theme — first a punch of hard, fresh oak, followed by a tempering note of floral incense. It’s quite a bizarre twist for a Garrison Bros. product, a chewy sweetness building as the body develops, ultimately evoking notes of toasted coconut, milk chocolate, and a touch of menthol. Increasingly minty on the finish, the whiskey winds its way away from sherry and toward duskier, huskier territory. As things develop, coffee and cherry notes become more prominent and sustained, with a curious hint of pistachio and ample, lingering chocolate on the finish. Definitely a twist on the GB formula. 110 proof. B+ / $150

Garrison Brothers Ranch Reserve Bourbon PX Review

For all the wine and fruit in the Oloroso expression, the PX version blows that out of the water. Stick your nose in the glass and it perks up right away: intensely nutty, leathery, raisiny, it’s a heady experience that pours on baking spice notes, especially cloves and ginger, all filtered through a thick skein of oak charred black.

The palate tells a similar story. Quite sweet and wholly wine-soaked, lush with raisins but more prominently dates and dried figs. Candied and laced with caramel and chocolate, this is one of the most decadent Garrison Brothers whiskeys I’ve ever encountered. Thick and unctuous, the whiskey drapes over the tongue like oil, turning toward maple syrup and more chocolate sauce as it develops. “Luxurious” is a word used by Garrison Bros. to describe this experience, and it couldn’t be more perfect.

The decadence and sweetness don’t last forever. Eventually the whiskey has to come back down to earth, where a sharper, wood-driven character awaits. That Texas heat can only be ignored for so long, and the conclusion is hot and tight, tannic oak rearing back like a bronco. Water helps to tame that finish, but it also perforates what comes before, dulling the fruit, taking the whole affair down a notch. Be careful with your water dosage, and you may well find yourself with a transcendent experience. 109 proof. A- / $150

The black bottle is inspired by Oaxaca’s barro negro pottery and is certainly striking on the shelf. Let’s give it a whirl. Mezcal El Silencio Espadin Review Designed to…

The post Review: Mezcal El Silencio Espadin appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
This was the first line extension of Mezcal El Silencio after its original Ensamble launch, this one made in San Baltazar, Oaxaca exclusively from espadin agave. The black bottle is inspired by Oaxaca’s barro negro pottery and is certainly striking on the shelf.

Let’s give it a whirl.

Mezcal El Silencio Espadin Review

Designed to be softer and less overtly smoky, this expression of El Silencio is true to its claims, more subtle on the nose than many modern mezcal expressions but certainly still part of the mezcal family, featuring notes of browning grass and creosote backed by a mix of dried herbs and hints of dark chocolate.

While the nose is quite savory, the palate finds a little sweetness, that chocolate emerging as touched with brown sugar and honey, some notes of cherry juice working their way into the mix. The spirit evolves in glass to reveal some of the salinity featured in the Ensamble release, particularly on the surprisingly lengthy finish. A spritz of lemon peel brightens up the outro, some sweetened mint syrup lingering on the conclusion.

It’s definitely a step up from the Ensamble and — good news — a significant price cut makes it much more appealing in its competitive space.

86 proof. NOM-AMMA78. Reviewed: Lot #001-25AM.

B+ / $38

title: Review: Suavecito Tequila Extra Anejo
summary:
Our first look at Suavecito was last year when Chris explored an Anejo Single Barrel that, on paper, is a bit of an outlier from the brand’s core lineup. The name Suavecito translates to “smooth” and shows up on every label in the portfolio outside of the single barrel expressions which, by Chris’s estimation, are…

The post Review: Suavecito Tequila Extra Anejo appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Our first look at Suavecito was last year when Chris explored an Anejo Single Barrel that, on paper, is a bit of an outlier from the brand’s core lineup. The name Suavecito translates to “smooth” and shows up on every label in the portfolio outside of the single barrel expressions which, by Chris’s estimation, are perhaps a bit too bold and dry to merit the descriptor.

Today, we’re looking at the tippy top of the “smoother” Suavecito offerings, an extra anejo made from 100% blue agave and aged in retired American oak bourbon barrels for an impressive five years – two years longer than required for the category. Like the rest of the non-single barrel Suavecito lineup, this isn’t technically a tequila by American standards due to its proof (70 proof is allowed in Mexico but 80 proof is the minimum in the U.S.). It also contains up to 2% unfermented agave nectar collected after roasting. Thoughts follow.

Suavecito Tequila Extra Anejo Review

The aroma is gentle and honeyed with notes of agave syrup, stewed peppers, and split vanilla bean. It’s sweet but not overly so, which is a bit surprising given the extended barrel aging and the addition of the agave nectar. Extra anejos can be butterscotch bombs, but this is almost closer to a standard anejo in profile with just a bit more bourbon barrel sweetness in the mix. As it opens, the savory notes bloom a bit more, adding some bell pepper and roasted agave to the bouquet.

The palate is where Suavecito’s mission for “smooth” really shows; for good and maybe not so good if you’re a tequila purist. This is a creamy, saccharine tequila that delivers zero hint of alcohol and little in the way of spiritous warmth. The sweetness is kept in check just enough to avoid being cloying but only just barely. Notes of dark honey, vanilla taffy, and agave syrup reinforce a dessert-like profile from sip to swallow. The midpalate manages to deliver a hint of coffee bean and a cooked agave note that is vaguely herbal before dissolving into a syrupy, gently peppery finish that is just short enough to keep the sweetness from feeling heavy. Suavecito makes no excuses for putting texture and temperature above flavor in their mission for the “smoothest” tequila. Purists probably aren’t their target audience, but there is probably enough flavor here for the occasional tequila drinker to appreciate. Its biggest fans will be newcomers to the category. And those with a serious sweet tooth.

70 proof.

B / $130

summary:

Ferrand’s new Pineau des Charentes is a fortified wine — and one of the most undersung delicacies of the Cognac region. If you aren’t familiar, Pineau des Charentes is made…

The post Review: Ferrand Pineau des Charentes Blanc appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Maison Ferrand may be known for making Cognac (and, of course, gin and rum as well), but its latest release isn’t a spirit at all. Ferrand’s new Pineau des Charentes is a fortified wine — and one of the most undersung delicacies of the Cognac region.

If you aren’t familiar, Pineau des Charentes is made in a method similar to Port, where freshly pressed grape must is fortified with Cognac before fermentation is complete, leaving the finished product naturally sweet and a little boozier than table wine. Ferrand’s is aged for a minimum of 18 months in oak barrels before bottling at 17% abv.

We received a bottle and put it through its paces.

Ferrand Pineau des Charentes Blanc Review

Pineau is always a treat to sample, and Ferrand’s is no exception. A bright nose exudes notes of mixed florals, honeyed pear, some citrus, and finally almonds, providing a truly beautiful collection of aromas to stick your nose into. As you sip, the initially floral-heavy wine leans more into the fruit, first lemon, then Meyer lemon, then tangerine. Soon, the affair turns peachy as the sweetness builds, finishing with a touch of apricot and a light hint of mint.

All told, it’s as delightful a bottle of Pineau as I can recall tasting in recent years. At this price, snap it up and sip it straight or mix it with tonic for an autumnal treat.

17% abv.

A- / $34

title: Review: Penelope Masters of Golf Hole 01, Riviera, and Blackberry Old Fashioned
summary:
Penelope has been extremely busy of late, putting out new whiskeys and RTD cocktails at a rapid clip. Today we’re looking at three of them, including a fruity bottled old fashioned and a pair of finished whiskeys. Penelope Architects of Golf Hole 01 Review The whiskey world loves no sport more than golf, so leave…

The post Review: Penelope Masters of Golf Hole 01, Riviera, and Blackberry Old Fashioned appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Penelope has been extremely busy of late, putting out new whiskeys and RTD cocktails at a rapid clip. Today we’re looking at three of them, including a fruity bottled old fashioned and a pair of finished whiskeys.

Penelope Architects of Golf Hole 01 Review

The whiskey world loves no sport more than golf, so leave it to Penelope to start a new series of whiskeys that will probably end up spanning 18 editions, or “Holes,” in the parlance of the brand. Three holes have been dropped from the start, each a 6 year old straight bourbon distinguished by a unique spin on its finishing technique. All three expressions are made from a 60% corn, 36% rye, 4% barley mashbill and were finished with additional American oak staves (a la Maker’s 46), the only difference among them being the length of the finishing time, which is measured in weeks. However, Penelope doesn’t disclose that finishing time for any of the offerings. In any case, we received only Hole 01 for review.

It’s a surprisingly lively and, at times, decadent bourbon, the stave finishing clearly having an outsized impact. The nose is bold and quite oak-forward, peppery and a touch smoky, but also big with cloves and grains with a heavy toast. Time in glass perks up a surprising fruit overtone — slightly pruny, with a dark chocolate glaze — which adds some lovely nuance to what could otherwise be a barrel-heavy experience.

The palate definitely drinks older than 6 years of age, smoldering chocolate and vanilla pushy against, again, a hefty fruitiness — blueberry, blackberry, touched with baking spice. This is one of those whiskeys that shifts fairly heavily as the finish arrives, becoming quite savory again, laden with wood and notes of furniture polish, then swinging back, at least a bit, toward anise and darker spice notes, with a reprise of clove and some anise.

I didn’t think this golf-themed whiskey was going to amount to much, but damn if it doesn’t make me want to pick up a 3-iron. 94 proof. A- / $80

Penelope Riviera Review

Riviera is the latest addition to Penelope Bourbon’s Cooper Series. It’s made by blending an 8-year-old American light whiskey with straight bourbon (no age stated), and is finished in rosé wine casks from Spain. If you remember Penelope Rose Cask Finish, this is something of a sequel (though Rose Cask Finish was a bourbon).

Riviera isn’t quite as delightful, a heavily charred nose giving the aromatics a thick smear of toasty wood, mildly smoky at times and heavy with gravelly asphalt notes and, curiously, a healthy touch of menthol. I’ll be quick to note that Rose Cask had a lot of the same aromas, but that things livened up quickly on its palate, showcasing effusive cherry and chocolate notes. There’s a lot of that here, but it takes longer to show its face, the woodiness maintaining long-term dominance. Eventually, the finish brightens up and pours on that fruit, offering more of a maraschino cherry overtone than anything else. It’s a close #2 to the original, but my heart still lies with the forebear. 94 proof. B+ / $80

Penelope Blackberry Old Fashioned Review

A fruity foil to Penelope’s Black Walnut Old Fashioned, this one really does wear those berries on its sleeve. The punch of blackberry isn’t entirely distinct, however. This could be a mix of blackberry with raspberry, strawberry, currant, and/or blueberry, but it’s really the dessert-like thought that counts, I suppose. Ample waves of chocolate and vanilla serve to temper the fruit before its sweetness gets out of control — though there’s a summery punch of maraschino cherry on the finish that feels perfectly on point with what’s come before. Simple, summertime sipping here. 38 proof. A- / $25

title: Review: Independence Brewing Native Texan and Oklahoma Suks
summary:
Independence Brewing was founded by two University of Texas alumni, so it makes sense that the founders would support the home team on this, the eve of 122nd edition of the Red River Rivalry against the University of Oklahoma, held annually at the Cotton Bowl in Dallas. But Independence bleeds burnt orange so much that…

The post Review: Independence Brewing Native Texan and Oklahoma Suks appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Independence Brewing was founded by two University of Texas alumni, so it makes sense that the founders would support the home team on this, the eve of 122nd edition of the Red River Rivalry against the University of Oklahoma, held annually at the Cotton Bowl in Dallas. But Independence bleeds burnt orange so much that they even put out to memorialize that rivalry, particularly the hatred for all things Oklahoma — a distaste that runs so thick that “OU Sucks!” is unofficially part of the Texas fight song.

Today we pour fresh pints of Independence’s most visible year-round offering, Native Texan, as well as the OU brew.

Independence Brewing Native Texan Review

Closer to a German style pilsner, with Hallertau Mittelfrüh hops pumped up to 36 IBUs. Brisk and foamy, this is a boldly malty beer that could well be Bavarian if you didn’t see the label, with a big pretzelly character that really fills the mouth. Light lemon and some cardamom notes sneak in as the beer warms up, the citrus becoming increasingly prominent as the finish arrives. Chewy but well-rounded, it’s touched with enough nuance to work whether it’s Oktoberfest or not. 5.2% abv. A- / $10 per six-pack

Independence Brewing Oklahoma Suks Review

A standard pilsner with a lighter sprinkling of Hallertau Mittelfrüh hops (just 10 IBUs). Considerably more straightforward, here the malt and cereal do all the heavy lifting, which leaves you with a rather sweet finish to deal with that ends up a little one note. Tasted side by side, the hops in Native Texan pull more of their weight than it originally seems, and Oklahoma Suks leaves the game with an overtly doughy, almost gummy quality on the tongue. Perhaps, of course, that’s the intent. Best enjoyed with a side of OU vs. Georgia highlights. 5% abv. B / $10 per six-pack

title: Review: Tequilas of Dos Hombres (Updated 2026)
summary:
In 2022, we covered the launch of Dos Hombres, a then exclusively mezcal brand backed by actors Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. At the time, we tipped our hat to the Breaking Bad stars for the super cool way they chose to focus on mezcal instead of the more ubiquitous and celebrity-saturated tequila category. But…

The post Review: Tequilas of Dos Hombres (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
In 2022, we covered the launch of Dos Hombres, a then exclusively mezcal brand backed by actors Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. At the time, we tipped our hat to the Breaking Bad stars for the super cool way they chose to focus on mezcal instead of the more ubiquitous and celebrity-saturated tequila category. But it was only a matter of time. This spring Dos Hombres jumped into the very crowded tequila game. To their credit, the brand is still going about things coolly with the same craft and impressive transparency that they apply to their mezcals.

We received a sample of their inaugural blanco tequila, which is produced in the village of Amatitan at Tequilera TAP Distillery from 100% blue weber agave by veteran Maestro Julio Cova who came out of retirement to guide the Dos Hombres project. The agave is crushed using a roller mill, cooked in a combination of autoclave (75%) and brick ovens (25%), fermented for an unusually long 72-96 hours, and then double distilled in stainless steel and copper. It rests for 30 days before bottling. Thoughts follow.

Update: Cranston and Paul have unsurprisingly taken the logical next step in tequila succession and added a reposado to the lineup. We’re adding that review here, and will add coverage of the eventual anejo release when it arrives.

Dos Hombres Tequila Blanco Review

Tequila may have been a comparatively boring move for the Breaking Bad boys, but damn if they didn’t nail this blanco. The nose shows some of the most depth I’ve encountered in an unaged tequila with creamy notes of sweet, roasted agave and cinnamon frosting. Undertones of fresh lime zest and grilled lemon add energy and brightness, and with time to open, accents of pink peppercorn further enhance an already warm and enticing aroma.

The palate is crisp and light with notes of mint and white pepper. The agave is unusually fresh in contrast to the typical roasted note you often find in tequila. In place of the traditional agave syrup or roasted pulp notes, this is noticeably brighter and more tropical. The midpalate is crisp and floral with orange oil and rosewater that transitions to freshly grated cinnamon and clove on a long, gently peppery finish. It works great in a classic tequila cocktail like a margarita with that crisp profile working wonders for balance. But it’s almost a shame to mix with it. 80 proof. A / $48 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Dos Hombres Tequila Reposado Review

Like the blanco, this tequila was produced in Amatitan, Jalisco from 100% blue weber agave using 72-96 hour fermentations and double distillation in copper and stainless steel. This expression was then aged a short three months in American oak – reportedly ex-bourbon barrels sourced from the Four Roses Distillery – and cut with deep earth volcanic water (sounds way cooler than “natural spring”). The final product was then allowed to rest a full 30 days in stainless steel to mellow and balance. Let’s check it out.

The nose is remarkable. I didn’t think they could improve on the blanco’s bouquet, but the barrel aging really has accentuated things. Top notes of gently cooked agave are silky and expressive, presenting with a rich, caramelized sweetness underpinned by soft baking spice and brown sugar. The citrus undertones show a surprising amount of freshness for a barrel aged spirit, coming through as just a little more candied than the blanco but still energetic and bright. The peppercorn notes from the unaged expression have softened to white pepper with a hint of smoke and minerality.

The palate is less transformed by the barrel, retaining the purity of this unusually fresh and gently spiced tequila with early notes of split piña, bruised mint, clove syrup, and candied pineapple. A light dusting of cinnamon sugar and notes of ginger snap cookies on the midpalate are the clearest evidence of the barrel aging, and even that gives way on the finish to a sweet, floral fadeout of orange marmalade and rosehip. Despite a memorable nose, I prefer the blanco just a bit more. Still, it’s an impressive next step in the Dos Hombres portfolio, and I look very much forward to sampling the anejo when it arrives. 80 proof. A- / $50

summary:

The post The Top 10 Wines for Winter 2027 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
For the first time in recent memory, the high temperature for the day was under 90 degrees here. That counts as fall in Austin, Texas, and is enough for us to break out our second top 10 wines list for the year. These 10 selections were picked with cooler weather in mind (and the meals that come with it) – though no one will bat an eye if you pop the cork on one of these before the temperature dips too far (or after it comes back up).

1. 2022 Terrazas de los Andes Extremo Malbec

Argentine malbec exists in two worlds: Affordable but wholly enjoyable entry-level wines on one hand, meticulously produced artisanal products on the other. As the name (and price) suggest, Terrazas de los Andes Extremo Malbec is in the latter camp, a serious wine produced at an altitude over a mile above sea level. The results are something else, a restrained wine that keeps wild herbs on the down low, fruit and oak well-integrated with silky tannin and bright acidity. Gentle spice notes linger on a finish so delightful you’ll forget what you paid for the experience. $200

2. 2023 Sassotondo Monte Calvo Ciliegiolo

Maremma flies a bit under the radar, but you’ll find some of Italy’s most nuanced wines produced in this Tuscan region. This one is made from ciliegiolo grapes (purportedly a progenitor of sangiovese, though this is disputed) which grow in rich volcanic soil. What Sassotondo has done with it is delightful, producing a light-bodied expression of fruity cherries, touched with almonds, flowers, and some peppery spice. While Chianti can be excessively tart, this wine offers a more balanced, almost creamy quality that really holds your attention. $45

3. 2020 Montefili Vigna Nel Bosco Chianti Classico Gran Selezione DOCG

Bosco is Italian for “woods,” and this Chianti Clasico bottling doesn’t just evoke the forest with its name, it also does in the glass. Lightly earthy and dusky, with a mix of green herbs and toasted spices, this smoldering wine moves into slightly sweeter, chocolate-driven character as the finish builds. In the end, the drinker is left with notes of cherry and plum to chew on. $61

4. 2021 Roederer Estate Clark Road Vineyard Anderson Valley

Vintage sparkling wines usually mean shelling out a small fortune for the luxury, but Roederer’s 2021 Clark Road Vineyard offering – 3/4 pinot noir and 1/4 chardonnay – is a delicious exception. One of my favorite wines from the operation, this fruity delight pairs dried apples and toasted almonds with ample salinity and late-game melon, all coming together to show off the delightful, citrus peel-driven finish. Great value. $55

5. 2023 X Novo Pinot Noir X Omni Vineyard

We had our first experience with X Novo this year and are hoping it won’t be the last. This brightly fruit-forward pinot keeps the focus on the purity of the berries, with smoldering terroir becoming increasingly visible as the wine develops in glass. The gentle tannins complement the wine beautifully, and even the touch of balsamic on the finish only serves to amplify the wine’s charms further. Like Cru Burgundy, made in California. $100

6. 2023 Oleandri La Scala Red Wine Napa Valley

This Left Bank Bordeaux-style blend throws a twist into the mix in the form of 4.5% petite sirah, which gives an already aggressive wine even more gravity and density. Nearly black in its opacity, the wine takes its core of currant and cocoa powder and pours on the earthiness, though the wine never approaches anything that tastes green or off. Air improves things further – consider decanting – allowing bright cherry elements to emerge. $80

7. 2023 The Prisoner Grail Stags Leap District

You surely know The Prisoner as a widely available (and much loved) red blend – but lately the brand has become the spearhead for a wide range of spinoffs, the latest being The Prisoner Grail, a luxe cabernet blend that approaches a whopping $200. It’s made from fruit from one of the most prized vineyards in Napa, Wappo Hill, and the significantly boozy wine doesn’t pull any punches. Bold currant, blackberry, and blueberry notes inform a very dense, undulating experience that is, quite naturally, balanced by gently tannic tobacco and graphite notes. The wine’s complexity never really ends, even as the finish finally fades out. $200

8. 2023 Prats + Symington Chryseia Douro DOC

Portugal is known for cheap whites and expensive Ports, but Chryseia stands as one of the country’s most noteworthy red table wines. A blend of Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca, the wine can stand up against any of the icons of the Old World, its elegant body driven by plum and cherry en route to a more brambly, slightly ashy finish. The structure is just about perfect, while the wine’s intensity is unyielding. $125

9. 2023 The Hilt Estate Chardonnay Santa Rita Hills

For my money, Chardonnay works better when there’s a bit of chill in the air than in the dead of summer, and while this beautiful wine leads with iconic lemon, apple, and pear notes, the fruit settles down into an autumnal groove, ultimately evoking thoughts of apple pie and coconut cream. Never overly woody nor saccharine in the slightest, it offers a clean and versatile experience that works both as a happy hour crowd-pleaser and as a mealtime companion. $50 [BUY IT NOW FROM WINE.COM]

10. 2022 Papapietro Perry Pinot Noir Russian River Valley Peters Vineyard

This striking Russian River Pinot dodges the trap that frequently sinks other Pinot Noirs from the region, its low-level notes of tea leaf and cola livened up by effusive cherry and boysenberry flavors, along with a grating of orange peel. The finish’s distinct chocolate and cinnamon notes provide an enchanting denouement to the wine’s lively attack. $69
